lessons.title: Articles — Il, La, Lo, L'
lessons.explanation: Italian articles agree with the noun's gender and the first letter of the following word. Masculine: il (before consonant), lo (before s+consonant, z, ps, gn, x), l' (before vowel). Feminine: la (before consonant), l' (before vowel). Plural: i, gli, le.
examples: il libro (the book — masc.)
la casa (the house — fem.)
lo studente (the student — starts with st)
l'amico (the friend — starts with vowel)
gli amici (the friends — masc. pl. before vowel)
lessons.tip: The choice of article depends on the gender AND the first sound of the noun. Il → i (pl.); lo → gli (pl.); la → le (pl.).

quiz.question: Which article goes with 'studente' (student, masc., starts with 'st')?
Which article goes with 'amica' (female friend, starts with vowel)?

lessons.title: Essere and Stare — To Be
lessons.explanation: Like Spanish, Italian has two 'to be' verbs. Essere: permanent states, identity, origin, time, passive. Stare: health, location (sometimes), progressive tense (stare + gerundio). Essere is far more common.
examples: Sono italiano. (I am Italian.) — essere, identity
Come stai? (How are you?) — stare, health
Sto mangiando. (I am eating.) — stare + gerund
È tardi. (It is late.) — essere, time
lessons.tip: When in doubt, use essere. Stare is mainly for health ('come stai?') and the progressive form.

quiz.question: Which verb do you use for 'I am Italian' (identity)?
Which verb do you use for 'I am eating' (progressive)?

lessons.title: Present Tense — Regular Verbs
lessons.explanation: Italian verbs have three groups: -ARE, -ERE, -IRE. Drop the infinitive ending and add personal endings. -ARE (parlare): parlo, parli, parla, parliamo, parlate, parlano. -ERE (credere): credo, credi, crede, crediamo, credete, credono. -IRE (partire): parto, parti, parte, partiamo, partite, partono.
examples: Io parlo italiano. (I speak Italian.)
Tu credi in me. (You believe in me.)
Lei parte domani. (She leaves tomorrow.)
Noi mangiamo insieme. (We eat together.)
lessons.tip: Italian subject pronouns (io, tu, lui…) are usually omitted — the verb ending shows who is speaking.

quiz.question: What is the 'noi' form of 'parlare'?

lessons.title: Avere — To Have
lessons.explanation: The verb avere (to have): ho, hai, ha, abbiamo, avete, hanno. Used for possession and as an auxiliary for passato prossimo.
examples: Ho un gatto. (I have a cat.)
Hai fame? (Are you hungry?) — lit. do you have hunger?
Ha una macchina. (He/she has a car.)
Abbiamo tempo. (We have time.)
lessons.tip: Avere is used for many body sensations: avere fame (be hungry), avere sete (be thirsty), avere sonno (be sleepy), avere paura (be scared).

quiz.question: How do you say 'I have' in Italian?

lessons.title: Passato Prossimo — Recent Past
lessons.explanation: The passato prossimo is the main past tense. Use avere or essere + past participle. Verbs of motion, reflexives, and some state verbs use essere. With essere, the participle agrees in gender and number with the subject.
examples: Ho mangiato la pizza. (I ate pizza.) — avere
Sono andato/a al mercato. (I went to the market.) — essere
Abbiamo visto il film. (We saw the film.) — avere
Sono arrivati tardi. (They arrived late.) — essere, masc. pl.
lessons.tip: Verbs with essere: andare, venire, partire, arrivare, nascere, morire, stare, essere, rimanere, and all reflexive verbs.

quiz.question: Which auxiliary does 'andare' use in passato prossimo?

lessons.title: Adjective Agreement
lessons.explanation: Italian adjectives agree in gender and number with the noun they describe. Adjectives ending in -o: -o (masc. sg.) / -a (fem. sg.) / -i (masc. pl.) / -e (fem. pl.). Adjectives ending in -e have only two forms: -e (singular) / -i (plural) for both genders.
examples: un ragazzo alto (a tall boy)
una ragazza alta (a tall girl)
dei ragazzi alti (tall boys)
una casa grande / delle case grandi (a big house / big houses)
lessons.tip: Most descriptive adjectives follow the noun in Italian, unlike English: una macchina rossa (a red car).

quiz.question: What is the feminine plural of 'alto'?
How many forms does an adjective ending in '-e' (like 'grande') have?

lessons.title: Possessive Adjectives
lessons.explanation: Italian possessive adjectives (mio, tuo, suo, nostro, vostro, loro) agree in gender and number with the thing possessed and are usually preceded by a definite article: il mio libro, la mia casa. 'Loro' is invariable.
examples: il mio libro (my book)
la mia amica (my friend — fem.)
i tuoi genitori (your parents)
la loro casa (their house)
lessons.tip: Unlike English, Italian possessives usually need the article too: not just 'mio libro' but 'il mio libro.'

quiz.question: Which article-possessive combination means 'my house' (casa, fem.)?
Which possessive adjective never changes form?

lessons.title: Comparatives and Superlatives
lessons.explanation: Italian comparatives use più/meno...di (more/less...than) or così...come / tanto...quanto (as...as). Relative superlatives use il/la più/meno + adjective. Some adjectives have irregular forms: buono→migliore, cattivo→peggiore.
examples: Lei è più alta di me. (She is taller than me.)
Questo libro è interessante quanto quello. (This book is as interesting as that one.)
È il ragazzo più intelligente della classe. (He is the smartest boy in the class.)
Questo gelato è migliore dell'altro. (This ice cream is better than the other.)
lessons.tip: Use 'di' before nouns/pronouns in comparisons (più alta di me) but 'che' when comparing two adjectives or clauses.

quiz.question: How do you say 'more...than' comparing two nouns in Italian?
What is the irregular comparative of 'buono'?

lessons.title: Congiuntivo — Subjunctive
lessons.explanation: The congiuntivo expresses doubt, wish, emotion, or uncertainty in subordinate clauses after 'che'. Present congiuntivo of -ARE verbs: parli, parli, parli, parliamo, parliate, parlino (note: io/tu/lui share same form).
examples: Voglio che tu venga. (I want you to come.)
È importante che studi. (It's important that you study.)
Penso che sia difficile. (I think it is difficult.)
Benché piova, usciamo. (Although it is raining, we go out.)
lessons.tip: The congiuntivo is triggered by expressions of desire, emotion, doubt, and impersonal expressions.

quiz.question: Which phrase triggers the Italian congiuntivo?

lessons.title: Imperfetto — Imperfect Tense
lessons.explanation: The imperfetto describes ongoing, habitual, or background past actions and descriptions, contrasting with the passato prossimo's completed events. Endings for -ARE verbs: -avo, -avi, -ava, -avamo, -avate, -avano. Essere is irregular (ero, eri, era...).
examples: Da bambino, giocavo sempre fuori. (As a child, I always used to play outside.)
Faceva bel tempo quel giorno. (The weather was nice that day.)
Abitavamo a Roma. (We used to live in Rome.)
Mentre lei leggeva, io cucinavo. (While she was reading, I was cooking.)
lessons.tip: Use imperfetto for descriptions and habits, passato prossimo for specific completed events — they often work together in narration.

quiz.question: Which tense describes habitual or ongoing past actions?
What is the 'io' imperfetto form of 'essere'?

lessons.title: Reflexive Verbs
lessons.explanation: Italian reflexive verbs use a reflexive pronoun (mi, ti, si, ci, vi, si) before the conjugated verb, indicating the subject acts on itself. Common reflexives: alzarsi, lavarsi, vestirsi. They always use essere in the passato prossimo, with the participle agreeing with the subject.
examples: Mi alzo alle sette. (I get up at seven.)
Lei si lava le mani. (She washes her hands.)
Ci vestiamo velocemente. (We get dressed quickly.)
Si sono svegliati tardi. (They woke up late.)
lessons.tip: Reflexive verbs always take 'essere' in the passato prossimo, and the past participle agrees with the subject's gender and number.

quiz.question: Which pronoun goes with 'noi' in reflexive verbs?
Which auxiliary do reflexive verbs use in the passato prossimo?

lessons.title: Futuro Semplice — Future Tense
lessons.explanation: The futuro semplice expresses future actions, formed by adding endings (-ò, -ai, -à, -emo, -ete, -anno) to a modified infinitive stem (drop the final -e, and -are verbs change the 'a' to 'e'). Some verbs have irregular stems: essere→sar-, avere→avr-, andare→andr-.
examples: Parlerò con lei domani. (I will speak with her tomorrow.)
Sarai felice. (You will be happy.)
Avremo tempo. (We will have time.)
Andranno in Italia l'estate prossima. (They will go to Italy next summer.)
lessons.tip: For -are verbs, the 'a' of the infinitive ending changes to 'e' before adding the future endings: parlare → parler-.

quiz.question: What is the 'io' futuro form of 'parlare'?
What is the irregular future stem of 'essere'?

lessons.title: Periodo Ipotetico — Conditionals
lessons.explanation: Italian conditional sentences have three types. Real (possible): se + present → future. Unlikely: se + imperfetto congiuntivo → condizionale presente. Impossible (past): se + trapassato congiuntivo → condizionale passato.
examples: Se studio, prendo un bel voto. (If I study, I get a good grade.) — real
Se avessi tempo, verrei. (If I had time, I would come.) — unlikely
Se avessi studiato, avrei superato. (If I had studied, I would have passed.) — impossible
Se piove, resto a casa. (If it rains, I stay home.) — real
lessons.tip: Match the verb forms: real = present/future; unlikely = imperfect subj./conditional; impossible = past perfect subj./past conditional.

quiz.question: For an 'unlikely' Italian conditional, what tense goes in the 'se' clause?

lessons.title: Voce Passiva — Passive Voice
lessons.explanation: The Italian passive voice shifts focus to the recipient of an action, formed with essere (conjugated in the appropriate tense) plus the past participle, which agrees with the subject. The agent, if mentioned, is introduced with 'da'.
examples: La casa è costruita da un famoso architetto. (The house is built by a famous architect.)
Il libro è stato scritto da lei. (The book was written by her.)
Le lettere sono spedite ogni giorno. (The letters are sent every day.)
La porta è stata aperta. (The door was opened.)
lessons.tip: The past participle in the passive always agrees in gender and number with the subject, just like with essere in the passato prossimo.

quiz.question: Which verb is the standard auxiliary for the Italian passive voice?
Which preposition introduces the agent in a passive sentence?

lessons.title: Pronomi Relativi — Relative Pronouns
lessons.explanation: Italian relative pronouns connect clauses: 'che' (who/that/which) is invariable and covers both subject and object roles; 'cui' is used after a preposition (a cui, di cui, con cui); 'il quale/la quale/i quali/le quali' can replace che or cui for clarity and agrees in gender and number.
examples: L'uomo che parla è mio padre. (The man who is speaking is my father.)
Il libro che leggo è interessante. (The book that I am reading is interesting.)
La persona a cui ho scritto è mia zia. (The person to whom I wrote is my aunt.)
Il film di cui parliamo è famoso. (The movie we are talking about is famous.)
lessons.tip: Use 'che' for direct subject/object roles; switch to 'cui' whenever a preposition is required before the pronoun.

quiz.question: Which relative pronoun is used after a preposition?
Is 'che' variable (does it change form) in Italian?

lessons.title: Trapassato Prossimo — Pluperfect
lessons.explanation: The trapassato prossimo describes an action that happened before another past action ('had done'), formed with the imperfetto of avere or essere plus the past participle. It follows the same auxiliary-choice and agreement rules as the passato prossimo.
examples: Avevo già mangiato quando è arrivata. (I had already eaten when she arrived.)
Era partita prima del nostro arrivo. (She had left before our arrival.)
Avevamo finito il lavoro. (We had finished the work.)
Si erano svegliati presto. (They had woken up early.)
lessons.tip: Think of the trapassato prossimo as 'one step further back' than the passato prossimo — it sets up a past-before-the-past sequence.

quiz.question: What auxiliary tense forms the trapassato prossimo?
What does the trapassato prossimo express?
options: an action before another past action
